about: The corrections this site has asked other publishers to make, kept by liaison@php.newsroom (brief: admin/content/briefs/2026-10-22__brief__the-corrections-liaison.md; desk: admin/liaison/README.md). Every request starts from a fact-check finding or contradiction in data/factcheck.json, quotes the publisher only from a capture in the evidence vault, and is on this site before any message is sent. The editor sends each request personally, from the email drafted under it (the editor's decision, 24 October 2026); no agent writes to a publisher.

statuses.means: Written from a fact-check record; not yet read by the editor
Waits on something named in blocked_by: usually an open finding against this site's own wording on the same point
The editor has read it and said it may go; not sent
The mail agent sent it to the publisher's corrections channel; the log has the time
The publisher replied without a change yet
The publisher changed the text; a new capture shows it
The publisher answered and kept the text; their reason is recorded
Fourteen days after sending, no answer; nothing more is sent

requests.point: The headline says the flaws affect 70% of the Internet; the post's own body says PHP powers 70% of all websites.

said.words: PHP2Shell: AI uncovers critical RCE vulnerabilities affecting 70% of the Internet
a popular general-purpose scripting language that powers 70% of all websites in the world.
a decade-old PHP Core vulnerability reaching CVSS 9.2 severity impacting 70% of the Internet.

requests.evidence: The 70% is the usual web-technology survey figure: the share of websites whose server-side language is known that use PHP (Cloudflare links it to W3Techs; Tenable and Imperva name W3Techs, at 69.3% and over 69%). It is a share of websites, not of hosts, traffic or the Internet, and it counts sites that use PHP at all, not installations running an affected version. Every outlet in our evidence vault that carries the figure traces back to this post.
requests.suggested: PHP2Shell: AI uncovers critical RCE vulnerabilities in PHP, the language behind about 70% of websites whose server-side language is known

requests.point: The live page puts "roughly 70%" in quotation marks as Wiz's estimate; Wiz's own words have no "roughly", and the 70% is a share of websites using PHP, not a measure of how much of the internet is affected.

said.words: with cyber-security firm Wiz estimating that "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to independently verify that figure.

requests.evidence: The words in quotation marks are not in either capture of Wiz's own words: the blog headline and the X post say '70% of the Internet', the blog body says '70% of all websites in the world'. The figure itself is a survey's share of websites whose server-side language is known that use PHP, not a share of the internet affected. The BBC's own caveat, that it could not verify the figure, is right and is kept in the suggestion.
requests.suggested: with cyber-security firm Wiz saying the flaws affect "70% of the Internet", a figure that matches surveys of how many websites use PHP rather than a count of vulnerable systems, and that the BBC has been unable to independently verify.

requests.point: The post says PHP2Shell "is now being broadly exploited in the wild"; the same post says it is unclear whether any of the attempts it saw would have succeeded. Readers, and WIRED's headline, take "exploited" to mean successful attacks.

said.words: PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.
Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems.

requests.evidence: AWS's sensors saw exploitation attempts, before and after the release; its own post leaves open whether any succeeded. The PHP Foundation told WIRED it knows of no successful remote code execution, CISA had not observed exploitation, and no named organisation has said it was compromised (this site's /compromise/ page). This is a request to clarify a word, not to change a finding.
requests.suggested: PHP2Shell exploitation attempts are now widespread in the wild; whether any have succeeded against real systems is not yet known.

requests.point: The headline and standfirst state 22 million vulnerable servers as a fact; the article's own body gives it as Palo Alto Networks' count of instances potentially vulnerable.

said.words: PHP2Shell: 22M exposed servers at risk as emergency patches released
Palo Alto Networks said Wednesday it had identified more than 22.6 million exposed instances potentially vulnerable to the PHP2Shell flaws.

requests.evidence: The body is right: Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 counted instances that are potentially vulnerable, and has not published its method. The headline and standfirst drop both the attribution and the 'potentially'. Censys, which publishes its method, counted 1.57 million unpatched hosts among the 1.58 million whose PHP version it could read. TechTarget Japan's translation carries the same figure as a fact (R-011).
requests.suggested: PHP2Shell: Palo Alto counts 22M exposed instances potentially at risk as emergency patches released

not_asked.words: With 70 percent of the Internet affected, the impact of PHP2Shell cannot be overstated
not_asked.why: CRN quotes Wiz's own words, attributed to Wiz. The request goes to Wiz (R-001).
The headline reports what security firms reported (watchTowr: 'exploitation in the wild'), and the body says plainly that it is unclear whether the attacks succeeded.

not_asked.words: with confirmed exploitation on widely deployed software including WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, phpMyAdmin, Nextcloud, and Magento
not_asked.why: The researchers did confirm code execution against these applications in their own tests; 'exploitation' is ambiguous rather than wrong, and this site's own claim used the same words until 24 October.
